From the “totally predictable consequences” department comes news that Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s rent freeze is drying up financing for distressed rent-regulated properties, including nonprofit providers.

The result? Less maintenance, more foreclosures and higher market-rate rents: Socialism delivers its usual disasters, in other words.

Lenders, from local community-development nonprofits all the way up to federally chartered mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, are toughening lending standards for rent-regulated buildings because the rent freeze just choked their expected income.

That is: Lenders expect to get their money back, with interest — these borrowers will now have less revenue coming to make payments.

News site The City Reporter just discovered that the rent freeze has made it impossible for landlords to get financing, unless the building has a significant number of market-rate units on top of its rent-regulated ones (in which case, market-rate renters pay extra to subsidize the cost of their rent-regulated neighbors).

With no market-rate tenants to eat the rising costs of labor, energy, taxes, insurance and materials, plus higher interest rates, owners of 100% rent-regulated buildings are out of luck.

Socialist housing advocates like Democratic Socialists of America co-chair Gustavo Gordillo laugh, smarmily encouraging struggling landlords to “pull themselves up by their bootstraps” and smirking that the Constitution doesn’t guarantee them “double digit” returns on their investments.

Of course, the socialists want private landlords to give up so their buildings can be turned over to politically connected nonprofits who’ll take over city housing.

Mamdani housing guru Cea Weaver’s New York State Tenant Bloc said it explicitly in July: “If landlords can’t maintain their buildings, tenants will.

“The Mayor’s Housing Plan directs $2.2 billion to taking housing off their hands. Tenants are organizing to defend our communities and reclaim our homes.”

The socialists can’t even blame greedy capitalists, since not-for-profit lenders are tightening standards, too.

This mess was totally predictable, and was widely predicted, in these pages and elsewhere.

Mamdani and his socialist-dreamer team went ahead anyway; maybe they really believe  they can rewrite the laws of economics and human psychology at will.

Or maybe they figure that, whenever socialism fails, they can just insist that the answer is more socialism.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Team Trump’s war on fraud is saving billions by purging people who don’t deserve benefits from programs like Medicaid, food stamps and Obamacare.

Most Americans would call that a victory, but Democrats call it heartless.

And in blue states like New York, the spending keeps soaring, fraud be damned.

As Unleash Poverty notes, 5.5 million fewer people get food stamps through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program since President Donald Trump took office — a 13% drop.

That’s an incredibly welcome reversal: Over the past 20 years, enrollment figures doubled.

Taxpayers can thank Trump & Co. for expanding the program’s work-or-study requirements for able-bodied Americans and for stepped up enforcement.

Medicaid, too, has seen 5.1 million (nearly 7%) fewer cases, again thanks to tighter rules and the Trump fraud crackdown.

Obamacare enrollment is down 4.6 million, reflecting the steep drop in “ghost” policies — i.e., those linked to people who never file claims, and may not even know they have insurance as other parties profit from the government subsidies spent in their name.

The shift in trends is long overdue and offers hope that fraudsters won’t keep robbing billions from taxpayers.

Yet Democrats and their allies use the drops to pretend Republicans are pushing grandma off the cliff.

“They took away Medicaid for people who need it most,” one Washington state senator gripes in a recent pro-Democrat ad.

“People Are Losing Food Assistance as the harmful 2025 Republican Reconciliation Law Is Implemented,” wailed the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities’ SNAP Tracker.

Flat-out lies: Purging fraudsters is essential to ensure enough money for “people who need it most.”

In New York, by contrast, the goal is to bloat the welfare rolls — and spend as much taxpayer cash as possible. That’s the Dems’ definition of “victory.”

Subscribe to our daily Post Opinion newsletter!

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Over the past five years alone, Bloomberg reports, state Medicaid outlays have jumped by $45 billion, or more than 50%, to a jaw-dropping projected $134 billion this year.

A key reason: fraud, exactly what Trump is trying to stamp out.

Over the past year, Trump’s Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services czar Dr. Mehmet Oz has been probing more than 100 sites in New York for Medicaid fraud.

Spending on New York’s Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program, which lets friends and family members collect payments for providing home-care services, mushroomed from less than $1 billion in 2016 to more than $11 billion in 2024

All before Trump returned to office — and reflecting enormous fraud; even Democrats admit that, though they make no serious attempt to curb it.

Which puts the lie to their claim that GOP cuts are hurting those who need help most.

If they truly cared about such people, they’d join in the fight against fraud — and help protect money meant for them.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

C.J. Gardner-Johnson is out of a job.

Just one day after serving a one-game suspension for spitting in the direction of the Raiders’ Brock Bowers last month, the Bills released Gardner-Johnson, according to The Athletic’s Joe Buscaglia.

Gardner-Johnson, 28, played six games for the Bills this season after signing a one-year, $6 million deal with the team over the offseason.

The safety had 26 tackles and an interception across his six appearances with Buffalo.

After the incident, Gardner-Johnson apologized to Bowers, his teammates and both organizations.

“There is no excuse for my actions, and I take full accountability,” Gardner-Johnson wrote, adding that spitting on Bowers was “inappropriate” and “unnecessary.”

His release comes after a turbulent 2025 season, during which he spent time with three different clubs.

After just three games, Gardner-Johnson was released by the Texans following “friction behind the scenes” and reported frustration from the player over his role and “wanting to blitz more.”

CJ Gardner-Johnson just did a Jalen Carter and spit on a player.He was ejected pic.twitter.com/C6BALpIABj

He would then join the Ravens but never appear in a game for the team before heading to Chicago and playing 10 games for the Bears.

The incident with Bowers was far from the only on-field spat Gardner-Johnson has been involved in throughout his career.

In 2024, he was ejected from a game against the Commanders after receiving two unsportsmanlike conduct penalties, then flipped off Washington fans as he left the field.

In 2020, as a member of the Saints, Gardner-Johnson was accused of spitting on Bears receiver Javon Wims, who punched him twice during an altercation.

He also made headlines following the Eagles’ Super Bowl victory in February 2025 for posting a crude social media message about Travis Kelce and his ex-girlfriend, Kayla Nicole.

What does a losing candidate do the day after the election?

Unfortunately, I know the answer firsthand.

A lifetime ago, it seems, I ran for Congress in Skokie, Illinois, the town where I spent most of my childhood.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

It is a deep-blue suburb of the deep-blue city of Chicago. The district, at the time, included the university town of Evanston, plus the far northern neighborhoods of the city itself, along the glittering lakefront.

Growing up, I was curious about politics. In college, I was a left-wing Democrat, and worked as an intern for then-Sen. Carol Moseley-Braun in Chicago.

I imagined running for Congress one day, but not as a Republican.

Fast-forward more than a decade. With some real-world experience behind me, I “came out” as a conservative in law school.

One day, Barney Frank, the late Massachusetts congressman, came to Harvard to lecture about the global financial crisis.

Frank spent his speech blaming Republicans. When I asked him how much responsibility he had for the crisis, since he was the chair of the House Financial Services Committee, he blew up at me. I kept my cool and we argued for about five minutes.

The video of our confrontation went viral, and soon the Illinois Republican Party called. Would I consider running for Congress back home?

Sure, I said. At that point I had already signed up to take the bar exam in California, but like many of my classmates during the recession, I didn’t have a job yet.

Plus, it was a unique opportunity to make a difference.

I knew my chances were slim: The last Republican to win in a city of Chicago district had only done so because the Democrat had been indicted for corruption.

But the incumbent in my district, Jan Schakowsky, had a few scandals that the media had overlooked. Perhaps in a “wave” election — like the Tea Party campaign of 2010 was shaping up to be — I might catch lightning in a bottle.

I launched my campaign with nothing — no money, no staff, just a couple of volunteers. I had to learn how to ask strangers to write checks.

I went to the national Republican headquarters and asked for opposition research on my opponent. They had never bothered.

So I did my own digging. And I began to find links between my opponent and the aggressive campaign by the Obama White House to sell Obamacare to the public.

A brilliant impresario named Andrew Breitbart had just launched a conservative news website in LA. He loved the story, and shopped it to Glenn Beck, then of Fox News. Beck used the story to connect the political dots between Obama’s Chicago and the DC swamp. He ran it for two weeks.

I started raising money. I hired staff, including a one-armed political veteran named Paul Miller.

Miller told me to start knocking on doors and greeting commuters at train stations. I wouldn’t meet everyone in the district, but I would “get my name out.”

Our opponent started making mistakes. She did a fundraiser with the famous White House correspondent Helen Joseph, who posed for photos with big donors.

A few weeks later, with the photos already in the mail, Joseph outed herself as a rabid antisemite.

Schakowsky also backed a new, far-left Jewish group called J Street, which took anti-Israel positions. That irritated residents of the heavily Jewish district.

It also convinced my former professor Alan Dershowitz, then a staunch Democrat, to weigh in. He came to Chicago for a fundraiser. I was the first Republican he had ever backed.

Now we had enough money for a real campaign.

I reached out to Paul Ryan, then an up-and-coming Republican with bold ideas about reforming Social Security and Medicare. He agreed to do a fundraiser. The media didn’t turn up — journalists didn’t dare cross Schakowsky — but hundreds of donors did.

The campaign was roaring. Commercials, rallies, debates. Conservatives started coming out of the woodwork to volunteer. Schakowsky, who normally directed volunteers to other districts, kept them in her own. That would help other Republicans win in neighboring districts.

On election night, as supporters gathered in a hotel ballroom, I watched results come in.

The race was called in an hour. Schakowsky didn’t take my concession call.

With a lump in my throat, I gave a speech thanking everyone.

The next day — at Miller’s direction — I was out at the train stations again. I shook hands; I thanked strangers for the opportunity to run.

That’s what you do the day after you lose. You thank the voters.

And then, you pick up the pieces.

I called friends in Washington. No jobs there.

But I had a California law license. I called Andrew Breitbart.

I lost in Chicago, but I won a new life in LA.

Joel Pollak is the Opinion editor of the California Post.

news.originalContent:
With control of the US Congress on the line, results from Tuesday’s races will have marked implications for the country.

After a full day of voting, the first polls have begun closing in the consequential US midterm elections.

Control of the US Congress is on the line, with all 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats up for grabs.

Democrats, who have campaigned on promises to combat the country’s rising cost of living and end the US-Israel war on Iran, are eyeing a return to power in the US House. The party is also optimistic it could recapture control of the US Senate from Republicans when all ballots are counted.

The first clues to how the midterms may affect each party will appear in the US state of Kentucky’s highly competitive sixth congressional district, where polls closed at 6pm ET (23:00 GMT).

In the conservative district, which includes the state’s second-largest city, Lexington, Democrats have invested heavily in the campaign of US Navy veteran Zach Dembo, who is running against a Trump-backed physician and former state lawmaker, Ralph Alvarado.

If Republicans hold the seat, it could signal how the party may perform in other races across the country.

Results from all of the day’s races will continue to come in throughout Tuesday evening. But some may not be known until Wednesday, or later, as more states finish voting and officials start releasing their vote counts.

Follow all the returns on Al Jazeera’s live results page.

news.originalContent:
Barca took early lead through Lamine Yamal before Raphinha continued fine goal-scoring form with a second-half brace.

Raphinha struck twice to propel Barcelona to a 3-0 Champions League win over visitors Aston Villa on Tuesday, ending the English side’s perfect start to the football competition.

Five-time winners Barcelona took an early lead through Lamine Yamal before Raphinha continued his fine goal-scoring form with a second-half brace.

Barca bounced back after defeat to champions Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) in their previous European outing to stay in the hunt for a top-eight league phase berth.

Manager Unai Emery’s Villa competed well in the first half, but were eventually undone by Barca’s greater ability in the final third.

The Champions League anthem was not played before the game, as a mark of respect for Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died of a cardiac arrest on Tuesday morning after an on-pitch collision in a Spanish second-division match the previous day, provoking shock across the football world.

“Yes, it was [a good win]; I want to dedicate this win to the fans, but today I don’t want to talk about football, I want to send a message to the family of Jesus – may he rest in peace,” Raphinha told Movistar.

“This can happen to anyone; it’s very tough … you’re going to play a game, and the same thing can happen to you…

“From the club, I want to send a message of strength to the family.”

Villa captain John McGinn had only visited Camp Nou once previously, on a summer holiday as an eight-year-old, and might have expected better weather than the downpour both teams were subjected to.

The skipper might also have expected a more focused start, with Villa handing Barcelona the lead in the seventh minute.

The Spanish champions pressed Aston Villa extremely high, and Joao Gomes played a poor pass straight to Yamal in his own box. The 19-year-old winger gladly took the gift and stroked past Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki.

Emery, who endured one of the worst nights of his career away at Barca when helming PSG in 2017 during a 6-1 defeat, may have feared the worst.

However, Villa reacted strongly, and Matty Cash had a vicious drive deflected narrowly wide before Joao Cancelo blocked Gomes’s effort.

Barcelona goalkeeper Joan Garcia was quick off his line to beat Nicolas Jackson to a dangerous through-ball.

Suzuki saved from Anthony Gordon as Villa again struggled to bring the ball out from the back under Barca’s pressing.

Garcia was called into action again by Johan Manzambi as the match lurched from end-to-end.

Barcelona extended their lead early in the second half when Fermin Lopez fed Raphinha, who showed quick footwork before finding the bottom corner.

Cancelo powered a strike narrowly over before setting up Raphinha for Barcelona’s third with a superb cross with the outside of his boot.

The Brazil winger, who has made the number nine position his own this season, pounced from close range for his 19th goal of the season across all competitions.

Yamal sent a shot skidding wide as Barcelona probed for a fourth. It did not come, but the Catalan giants were able to record a first Champions League clean sheet in 19 games.

Elsewhere on Tuesday, Bayern ‌Munich and PSG underlined their Champions ⁠League title ⁠credentials with victories over Atletico Madrid and Villarreal respectively, while Manchester United came ⁠from two goals down to snatch a dramatic win over AS Roma.

Bayern broke down a stubborn Atletico ⁠side in Madrid as second-half goals from Lennart Karl and Konrad Laimer secured victory, while PSG set a record as the fastest team to score four goals in ‌a Champions League match on their way to a 6-0 victory.

At Old Trafford, Matheus Cunha struck twice in quick succession after the break as United overturned a two-goal deficit to beat Roma 3-2, the comeback following protests by home supporters.

news.originalContent:
Over half a billion dollars have been spent on the Talarico-Paxton race for US Senate, which has been dominated by voter affordability concerns.

Houston, Texas, the US – Texas voters have begun casting ballots in a consequential US Senate race that has already become the most expensive in United States history.

All told, at least $573.2m had been poured into support for both Republican candidate Ken Paxton and Democratic candidate James Talarico ahead of the Tuesday, November 3 vote.

The figure has included at least $212m to support Paxton from billionaire Elon Musk, whose SpaceX company is based in southern Texas.

The sum made voters of varying political persuasions queasy as they cast their ballots in a race that has been defined by affordability issues.

“That kind of money is being spent on the wrong stuff,” said Rico Sanchez, a 40-year-old union sheet metal worker who voted for Democrats based on the sky-high cost of living.

“It’s about control,” he said.

Kasey Blanco, a 21-year-old who split his ballot, voting for Republican Governor Greg Abbott and Democratic US Senate candidate Talarico, echoed the sentiment.

“It’s kind of scary,” he said. “You see the extent that a lot of these politicians are trying to get into the game and distort the view.”

Political power “should be from the people, by the people”, Blanco said.

The record spending has included both funds raised by the campaigns, as well as outside spending.

Talarico has outpaced Paxton in campaign funding, raising $155m to Paxton’s $40m. Federal law limits fundraising from individual donors, who must identify themselves.

Separately, a huge amount of money has poured in via political action committees called super PACs, which can spend an unlimited amount in support of a candidate but cannot directly coordinate with campaigns.

Paxton has been the largest beneficiary of such spending, including $168m from Musk to the Senate Leadership Fund, which has gone almost completely to supporting the Republican candidate, according to a New York Times analysis.

The newspaper estimated that Musk, who briefly and controversially led US President Donald Trump’s federal cost-cutting panel, the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), had spent at least $212m on Paxton, noting it was likely an undercount due to so-called “dark money” spending. Trump’s MAGA Inc PAC has spent at least $10m to support Paxton.

The Lone Star Rising PAC, meanwhile, has spent at least $21m on Talarico.

With national eyes on Texas, both US Senate candidates gave their closing pitches late Monday.

Talarico seized on Paxton’s past corruption allegations as Texas attorney general, drawing attention to Musk’s spending spree as evidence of prioritising big money interests over everyday voters.

His campaign has regularly referenced the “Friday Night Lights” television show, the story of an underdog American football team.

A Talarico victory would represent the first time a Democrat has won statewide office in Texas since 1994, with the party long hoping to “turn Texas blue”.

“We’re going to do something extraordinary,” Talarico said from San Antonio. “We’re going to do something historic. We’re going to shock the billionaires, shock the world, when we take back Texas.”

Paxton has portrayed Talarico as antithetical to the ideals of Texas, which has been dominated by Republicans for three decades. The state’s low-tax, low-regulation model, mixed with conservative social policies, has long given it special significance in Republican mythos.

Paxton’s campaign has repeatedly referenced the 1836 Texas Revolution, an uprising against then-Mexican control.

“We’ve never been this close to losing everything that we hold dear – our jobs, our livelihoods, our way of life in Texas,” he said at an event in Collin County. “If Texas falls, we don’t have another Texas to move to.”

Casting her ballot on Tuesday, 46-year-old Texas voter Monique Orellana said she was uncomfortable with Musk’s spending.

“He’s pouring all that money out here, trying to get whatever he’s trying to get,” she told Al Jazeera.

Regardless of party, she wanted elected officials to do their job and represent the people.

“I would vote for Republicans if I felt they were gonna do what they said they were gonna do. Right now I’m not feeling it,” she said.

“Trump said he wasn’t going to start a war, and he did anyway. And he said he was going to fix the price of groceries on day one. They went up anyway,” she said.

Voter Luis Plazas, 58, said he was not as concerned about the election spending, but wanted to see the economy improve and a pivot on Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

Still, he said, he voted Republican down the ballot, a decision he said was motivated by his religious beliefs.

“I’m a Christian, so I believe in family values, and it seems like Republicans are more inclined to that,” he said.

“I’m not really happy with the contenders or who I voted for, but my main concern right now is conservative values.”

She criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as “arrogant,” and said of the Iran War in June, “Israel and the neocons want regime change at all costs, even if it takes U.S. boots on the ground.” More recently, she questioned whether Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed should condemn a political ad that blamed higher grocery prices on the amount of financial aid the U.S. sends to Israel. (RELATED: Horsemen Of The Neocon Apocalypse Reportedly Whispering In Trump’s Ear)

After one X user resurfaced the June clip in which Campos-Duffy dared to point out that Israel was making the negotiating process with Iran harder for the Trump administration, and another then claimed she had crossed over to the “dark side,” Campos-Duffy responded.

Fox News has a Rachel Campos-Duffy problem. For those still wavering or not totally sold on @RCamposDuffy’s disgusting comments from yesterday, watch the much worse things she said when filling in for Jesse in June. Many missed that Friday night show bec many hosts were out. https://t.co/ALFXTHIchM

“Calling for an end to war & a return to diplomacy & peace is crossing ‘into the dark side’?” she asked, before quoting a Bible verse. “‘Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness’ Isaiah 5:20.”

The replies to her post were largely unhinged, as users (and likely several bots) accused her of being an antisemite and endorsing El-Sayed.

“I don’t hate Israel,” she responded to one reply. “I hate forever wars. Many Israelis feel the same. Try keeping up with the politics there.”

Writing to a user who said Oct. 31, “You’re an ignorant antisemite, “closet Hasan Piker supporter,” and “Dumb beach [sic],” Campos-Duffy replied, “Not anti semite. Just anti war & America First.”

@nos_neb Not anti semite. Just anti war & America First.

The smear campaign got a bit more Orwellian with disgruntled Fox News viewer and CUNY law professor, Jeffrey Lax, complaining in the Washington Examiner on Tuesday that Campos-Duffy has committed wrong-think that cannot go unaddressed by Fox executives.

“Does Fox News have a Rachel Campos-Duffy problem? I think so and said so Sunday night, and I say it as a friend of this network that has been very good to me and on the issues that I hold dear,” he wrote. “I’ve appeared on Fox many times. I have watched its hosts consistently defend Israel and the Jewish people with moral clarity for years. That clarity is why Campos-Duffy’s positions need to be addressed. Fox’s most loyal viewers deserves to know where the network stands on its editorial positions and standards.”

With every single Fox host and on-air contributor defending the Iran War, Israel, Ukraine, and militarism more broadly, around the clock, during every single broadcast, one would think this supermajority sufficiently — and soothingly — confirms the worldviews of hawkish Republican viewers. Apparently not.

news.originalContent:
One of the most infuriating things about the Biden years was the shameless, nonstop insistence, from the president himself, Treasury Sec. Janet Yellen, and members of the White House economic council that the red-hot, post-COVID inflation was a temporary trend that would soon wane, thanks to the administration’s Inflation Reduction Act. No one bought the spin, because Americans have eyes and could see, very clearly, their grocery, gas, and utility bills steadily increasing as the country emerged from the pandemic. Yet, the administration’s gaslighting continued, unfettered. Look at the charts, they said. Look at the data! Inflation is temporary. It was Groundhog Day: an endless, recurring absurdity.

Of course, Republicans had an absolute field day, and slammed the Biden White House for lying to Americans about rising prices (as well as lying about the fact that Biden was senile, but that’s another story). But the early 2020s have come and gone, and now Republicans, still in power as of Tuesday, are stuck in a similar position as Biden and the Democratic Party were ahead of the 2022 midterms. The Iran War has triggered even higher prices, and global shipping costs appear to be getting more permanently expensive. Americans are paying a hefty price for another Middle East war, yet few Republicans have had the temerity to acknowledge — really acknowledge— not only their pain but how it is a direct result of a bungled military intervention. Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis is a rare exception. (RELATED: Hidden Cost Of War That Trickles Down To Your Grocery Bill Set To Explode In 2027)

news.originalContent:
(Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump revealed an agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to scrap billions in annual U.S. aid.

Trump appeared on Fox News’ “Fox and Friends” Monday for his last media appearance, as midterm election voting begins across the country.

.@POTUS on aid to Israel: "It gets cut off at the end of the year… They don’t need it… Israel is a very thriving country." https://t.co/iIJbOv2kgU

During the interview, Trump turned to the annual U.S. assistance provided to Israel, which is allocated primarily for the country’s military and security purposes. (RELATED: Israel’s Election Chaos Could Fuel A New Iran War Escalation)

“As far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal to give $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago. That we’re stopping, and they’re fine with it. Cause you know, because they have become a very successful country. They don’t need it. And we won’t be paying more [to] Israel,” Trump said.

“It’s just a wasted thing because we’ve already agreed that by the end of this year, we won’t be paying Israel. Now, we’ll help Israel if they need it. You know, they’ve been a great ally, and we’ve been the greatest of all allies to many countries,” he continued.

Fox and Friends host Brian Kilmeade interjected to clarify whether Trump meant the U.S. would no longer provide Israel with $4 billion worth of weapons.

Trump interrupted to discuss the U.S. having total control of the Strait of Hormuz and the power of the United States’ military before Kilmeade returned to the question of Israeli aid.

“When it comes to Israel aid — we understand that we have cut aid to Israel that we were giving them $4 billion, and you are no longer going to be giving them $4 billion?” Kilmeade asked. (RELATED: US Oil Plunges Below $100 On Hopes Of Iran Peace Deal)

“We were giving them $4 billion. We are. But it gets cut off at the end of the year,” Trump responded.

Kilmeade pressed the President, asking him “why” they are cutting the funding.

“Why? They don’t need it, Brian. I mean, I asked them, because they don’t need it, and because why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it? It’s a bad talking point,” Trump said.

Trump said he and Netanyahu had reached an agreement to end the assistance after discussing the issue for a couple of years. He added that the Israeli prime minister had raised the prospect of ending the aid himself.

Big news on Israel aid. Trump says he agreed with Netanyahu to end the $3.8B in annual military assistance to Israel. “We made a deal months ago that we’re stopping, and at there they’re fine with it… we won’t be paying any more Israel… We’ve already agreed that by the end of this year we won’t be paying Israel. Now, we’ll help Israel if they need it.” https://t.co/diBBC0ltLF

“We reached an agreement on that, and can I be honest with you? He brought it up,” Trump said, explaining that Netanyahu believed it would be “appropriate” for Israel to stop receiving the assistance. Trump acknowledged that he understood the issue was a “point of contention.” (RELATED: Multiple Mike Rogers Campaign Staffers Are Paid Agents For Israel, Report Shows)

Kilmeade again sought clarification on whether Trump was ending $4 billion in military assistance, including weapons and other hardware, or a direct financial payment.

“Four billion in any way you want to define it. You can consider it a barter, you can consider it military aid or cash. We give them billions of dollars in things and money, and they don’t need it,” Trump responded.

Trump shared an additional motivator for ending U.S. aid to Israel: “I am someone who would like to have a balanced budget. I would love to be able to balance out the budget, and I think I can do it.”

news.originalContent:

The Bears hype train is full steam ahead.

After a huge win on “Monday Night Football” over the reigning Super Bowl champion Seahawks, the Monster of the Midway have seen their own Super Bowl odds rise significantly.

At BetMGM Sportsbook, the Bears now have the third-shortest odds to win the Super Bowl at +900, behind the 49ers at +600 and the Bills at +550.

According to Christian Cipollini, a Senior Manager at BetMGM, 30 percent of the money wagered on the Super Bowl futures has landed on the Bears, which is the most for any single team over that span.

It has been a steady climb for coach Ben Johnson’s group, who opened at 25/1 this season and saw their odds shorten from 14/1 to 11/1 immediately after swinging a huge trade for star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons last week.

That move paid off almost immediately with Simmons registering six tackles, including a sack in his first game with Chicago.

But Chicago’s strength is its offense, led by quarterback Caleb Williams, who has made a leap this season.

The Bears have scored at least 30 points in all but one of his starts, a Week 2 loss to the Vikings in a rain-filled game that he left with a hamstring injury.

Williams ranks second in QBR (78.9) behind Brock Purdy and second in completion percentage (70.9) among qualified quarterbacks, and has moved from 12/1 to win NFL MVP to +800 over the past week, which places him fourth on the list behind Josh Allen (+150), Joe Burrow (+425), and Brock Purdy (+450).

As good as things have gone for Chicago in recent weeks, they still have an uphill climb as far as securing a top spot in the NFC.

They trail the Vikings (6-1) in the NFC North standings and are 0-2 against the division with losses to the Vikings at home and to the Packers at Green Bay.

They also have the toughest remaining strength of schedule in the NFL according to Tankathon, with two games against the Lions, the Bills on the road, the Jaguars, the Packers and the Vikings in Week 18.

If they can survive that gauntlet, they could see their odds continue to shorten heading into the postseason.

news.originalContent:

A California high school has abruptly shut down its entire football program for the rest of the season after allegations of misconduct involving varsity players sparked a police investigation and led to a student being cited for battery.

Fred C. Beyer High School in Modesto canceled all remaining games and practices for its varsity, junior varsity and freshman teams after administrators learned of cellphone footage allegedly showing misconduct within the football program, according to the Sacramento Bee.

The school’s head football coach, Mike Young, was also placed on administrative leave late last week, although officials have not disclosed why he was removed from his duties.

Modesto police launched an investigation after school administrators reported the allegations to authorities. Investigators reviewed video evidence and ultimately cited one player for misdemeanor battery.

“We are deeply troubled by allegations involving members of the Fred C. Beyer High School football program,” Modesto City Schools said in a statement Friday. “These allegations are extremely serious and have no place in our schools or athletic programs.”

The district has released few details about what allegedly happened, how many players may have been involved or whether additional students were harmed.

It also remains unclear whether Young was placed on leave because of accusations involving his own conduct, concerns about his supervision of the team or other circumstances.

School officials said they were conducting their own investigation to determine whether other students were involved and what disciplinary measures should follow.

The district has also made counseling and other support services available to student-athletes and emphasized that students and employees receive annual harassment-prevention training.

Anyone with information about the allegations has been urged to contact school administrators, the district or Modesto police.

The controversy comes after a series of troubling incidents at Beyer High School in recent weeks, including multiple student fights and a threatening social media post.

On Oct. 16, five fights erupted on campus, forcing administrators to place the school on lockdown as employees and police intervened, according to the Sacramento Bee.

Four of the altercations broke out simultaneously during lunch, while a fifth occurred later that day, district officials said.

Three students were transported to a hospital for medical evaluation, although authorities said they found no indication that weapons were involved.

In response, school officials increased security the following Monday and provided additional protection during a school dance that weekend.

The campus faced another scare after a Riverbank High School student allegedly posted a threat targeting Beyer on social media.

Modesto police cited the student but said investigators found nothing suggesting there was a genuine plan to carry out an attack.

“We do not believe that the Oct. 29 incident is connected in any way to the fights that took place earlier in the month,” Modesto Police Department spokesperson Herman Sahota told the Sacramento Bee.

Authorities have also not identified any connection between the threatening post and the allegations surrounding the football team.

The cancellation brings an early end to another disappointing season for Beyer’s Patriots, who had already been struggling on the field.

The varsity squad had recorded just one victory in nine games and lost all six of its league matchups before the district canceled the remainder of the season, according to MaxPreps.

The team has endured years of poor results, finishing without a single win in 2018, 2021 and 2022.

While the football season is over, the fallout from the allegations may not be.

The student cited for misdemeanor battery could still face further consequences pending a review by probation officials and prosecutors.

Sahota told the Sacramento Bee on Monday that police had not cited any additional students and had received no new witnesses or evidence.

He also confirmed that Young had neither been arrested nor cited in connection with the investigation.

Police could reopen their investigation if new information comes to light, according to The Bee.

Meanwhile, the district has not publicly confirmed whether its internal investigation is complete, what disciplinary action students may face or whether Young will return to the sidelines next season.

news.originalContent:

The eight unexpected joys of working on Christmas Day have been revealed – and they’re not all about the money.

A poll of 1,000 adults who’ve done a shift on December 25th saw the lack of pressure to have a perfect Christmas Day and not having to travel long distances rank highly among these perks.

More than a quarter (27 percent) also value not having to worry about cooking their festive dinner or cleaning up afterwards (19 percent).

Others cherish the peace, which comes from commuting on quieter roads (37 percent) and having some space from navigating family dynamics (15 percent).

But for 37 percent, the main draw is the chance to make Christmas special for someone else, while 25 percent enjoy giving back to their community.

For example, among healthcare workers, 45 percent cherish helping to make the day feel meaningful for those who can’t enjoy it with their loved ones.

The research was commissioned by Greene King, whose second annual Big Christmas Shift offers Christmas Day workers a free meal from 2nd to 5th December; they have until 16th November to sign up or to be nominated by loved ones.

Carried out through OnePoll, the research found that while they have worked a total of six shifts to date on average, the typical festive worker is now on their fourth Christmas in a row, with 21 percent having done 10 or more shifts during their career.

The findings follow a separate study by ONS which found 1.2 million people worked on Christmas Day in 2025, up from 1.1 million in 2018.

This latest study, however, identified the moments which stand out to those working in care or medical sectors specifically – these include comforting someone struggling and helping those who might otherwise have spent Christmas alone.

Others have helped people take part in a Christmas tradition (16 percent) or connect with their family (20 percent) on the day.

Among all workers polled, 30 percent cited how special it was to witness someone’s mood improve because of something they did or receiving an unexpected thank you (27 percent).

Many have even received a card (28 percent), gift (25 percent) or edible token of thanks (33 percent) on December 25th.

To make it possible for them to give back to their community on Christmas Day, the data also revealed how shift workers adapt their own celebrations to make it happen.

While some reschedule the entire day to spend fully with their family, either before (25 percent) or after (eight percent) the 25th, 79 percent have instead opted to set aside a few key traditions.

Such as having their Christmas dinner (45 percent), seeing extended family (37 percent), opening presents (31 percent), or going for a festive walk (18 percent).

Andrew Gallagher from Greene King, which has produced a video [https://youtu.be/scwNjvQgrlc] celebrating those who work behind the scenes and make Christmas happen, said: “Behind so many special moments that the rest of us enjoy, there are people giving up time with their loved ones to make Christmas special for somebody else.

“So, this year, we are giving Santa a little less of the credit and putting the spotlight on Britain’s real Christmas shift workers.

“Offering 30,000 free meals is our way of saying thank you to every person behind the scenes and giving them a chance to enjoy some well-earned festive cheer of their own.”

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The 49ers orchestrated a blockbuster trade ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline.

San Francisco landed defensive lineman DeForest Buckner in a deal with the Colts at the end of October, but the 49ers may not be done on the trade block.

On The Pivot Podcast, NFL insider Jordan Schultz discussed what fans can expect ahead of the trade deadline and he explained why San Francisco’s front office could have another trick up its sleeve.

“Last week, I talked about San Francisco and Chicago. Those were two teams that I thought would be really active. Now, the Bears landed [Jeffery] Simmons in a blockbuster. San Francisco got [DeForest] Buckner. So we were in on that,” Schultz said.

“But Ryan, I don’t think either team is done. I think the 49ers are still looking for a receiver and a pass rusher. I wouldn’t rule out another move for either team.

“There’s a lot of Khalil Mack buzz for both clubs. The Jets have made it clear they’re not looking to trade their stars, including Garrett Wilson. But there has been some curiosity around Breece Hall, so we’ll see what happens there.”

While running back is not a need for the Niners with Christian McCaffrey in place, wide receiver has been a glaring need.

“But the biggest name around the league that people are really starting to get curious about is George Pickens in Dallas,” Schultz said. “He’s playing on the franchise tag. He has not been utilized the same way as last year.”

Last season, Pickens earned his first Pro Bowl nod, reeling in 93 passes for 1,429 yards and nine touchdowns. This year, he has just 39 catches for just over 500 yards and two trips to the end zone.

All while the Cowboys’ season fades into oblivion.

San Fransisco has been decimated by injury at the receiver position. Mike Evans is expected back, as are rookie De’Zhaun Stribling and Deebo Samuel. But those are still unanswered questions. Never mind losing Christian Kirk and Ricky Pearsall for the season already.

The 49ers have reached the Super Bowl in recent years without the right pieces, but were unable to hoist the Lombardi Trophy. Perhaps San Francisco learns from history and remains aggressive on the trade market until the Nov. 10 deadline.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Milania Giudice’s best friend, Victoria Zardoya, had ketamine in her system at the time of her fatal fall in July.

The 20-year-old’s blood tested positive for ketamine — a dissociative anesthetic that has some hallucinogenic effects, per DEA.gov — and norketamine — a metabolite that is produced when the body breaks down ketamine, according to a medical examiner’s report obtained by TMZ.

Zardoya’s toxicology results also showed alcohol and etomidate, a medication used for general anesthesia.

The young woman’s death was ruled accidental and the cause was recorded as craniocerebral trauma, as she suffered skull fractures and bleeding around the brain from the tragic fall.

On July 24, Zardoya fell down a multi-level flight of stairs while she was exploring the Fort Dade ruins on Egmont Key near Tampa Bay, Florida.

She was airlifted to a nearby hospital in critical condition but sadly passed three days later from her injuries.

Want celebrity news as it breaks?

Zardoya grew up as a neighbor and close family friend to Giudice, also 20, and her famous family.

The “Real Housewives of New Jersey” star struggled with her BFF’s death — even making headlines in September for getting into a heated exchange with her mom, Teresa Giudice, and her oldest sister, Gia Giudice, while surrounded by cops at the Tampa International Airport.

Milania’s dad, Joe Giudice, told Page Six during an exclusive interview that Zardoya’s death “affected” his daughter “tremendously.”

“Losing someone you love is incredibly painful, and grief does not have a timeline,” the convicted felon, 54, told us.

“She has been trying to process that loss while also dealing with the pressures that come with growing up in the public eye,” he added.

Last month, Milania revealed she had been diagnosed with multiple mental health issues, including bipolar disorder, depression, anxiety, PTSD and ADHD, and had checked herself into a rehab center.

news.originalContent:

WASHINGTON — Daniel J. Sullivan, the independent Alaska Senate candidate with the same name as incumbent Republican Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan, remained missing on Election Day as President Trump accused him of committing a “criminal act.”

While serious candidates typically stump for votes in the final hours of the midterm election, the mysterious Sullivan was not holding campaign events — and was nowhere to be found.

“Decoy Dan,” a retired school teacher, was recruited to run by the campaign of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, the New York Times reported last week, prompting a Justice Department investigation and DOJ litigation to stall certification of the election results if Peltola wins.

Sullivan left his small hometown of Petersburg last Monday, CBS News reported, with a former student spotting him on a flight to Anchorage.

He did not respond to an email or text message from The Post on Tuesday. His voicemail played a lengthy Halloween-themed message.

Alaska has ranked-choice voting, which could protract tabulations if there isn’t a clear winner.

Although voters could in theory vote for both Sullivans, with the long-shot candidate’s votes being reallocated to the Republican through the ranked-choice process, GOP leaders are concerned about losing any votes with polls showing Peltola narrowly ahead or tied with the Republican.

“It’s a total fraud. It’s a fraud on the voters. And it’s a criminal act,” Trump said Tuesday morning in an interview with “Fox & Friends.”

There are four candidates who will appear on the ballot. A sample form shows that Sen. Sullivan is identified as the incumbent and a Republican; Peltola is identified as a Democrat; and the other Sullivan has no party label.

In a further twist, the fourth candidate, drywall contractor Gerald Heikes, is identified as a Republican.

Heikes told the Times that he was recruited “by a guy from the Midwest” who told him, “Hey, if you go and file to run for Senate, we’ll back you — we can’t give you money or anything, but we’ll make things happen for you.”

Concern about the lesser-known Sullivan and Heikes siphoning votes may be well-founded. The state’s Aug. 18 jungle primary, which featured candidates of all party affiliations, saw Daniel J. Sullivan take 2.5% of the vote and Heikes 1.1%, with both advancing to the general election.

The RealClearPolitics polling average shows Peltola leading the general election contest by 1 percentage point.

Concern about the lesser-known Sullivan and Heikes siphoning votes may be well-founded. The state’s Aug. 18 jungle primary, which featured candidates of all party affiliations, saw Daniel J. Sullivan take 2.5% of the vote and Heikes 1.1%, with both advancing to the general election.

The RealClearPolitics polling average shows Peltola leading the general election contest by 1 percentage point.

WHITE LAKE, Mich. — Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens said she has no regrets about voting for Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan as he defended her against the vicious attacks from members of her own party.

Stevens said it was “worth” voting a split ticket, supporting Democrats down the ballot except for Abdul El-Sayed in the Senate race.

“Voting is always worth it,” she told News Nation as she went into her polling place to cast her ballot.

And she expressed confidence her party would win the House majority on Tuesday, saying she’s already spoken to Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York.

“It’s the people’s day. And I’ve told this to our next speaker of the House, Hakeem Jeffries: It’s majority-makers day,” she said.

Democrats en masse disavowed Stevens for voting against El Sayed, whom she previously endorsed after losing to him in the contentious August primary by one point.

Several of them called on her to be thrown out of the party, said her political future was finished, and alleged she had been influenced by pressure from her Jewish fiancé, Jason Turkish, into supporting Rogers.

But Rogers defended her, calling her courageous and slamming the vitriol hurled her way.

“I’m disappointed in how vicious they’ve been,” Rogers told reporters at his polling place at St. Patrick Catholic Church in his congressional district.

“But I think that speaks to who the modern Democrat Party is. Here’s somebody who said, ‘I voted Democrat all the way down the list, except for one person who I think is too extreme for our state.’ That’s country over party. They ought to celebrate her courage and encourage her to continue to being a Democrat rather than trying to throw her out of the party, I mean, I’ve never seen such viciousness online.”

Rogers said El-Sayed, who is part of the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, is too extreme for Michigan. Several Democrats in the state have said they’ll be voting on a “split ticket,” supporting their party except in the Senate race.

“She was just a part of multiple Democrats who have come out and said Abdul El-Sayed is too extreme for this state. That part didn’t get covered much, but I think she was obviously the highest profile, and took a lot of courage for her to do that,” Rogers said.

“I’m proud of her for doing what she believed was the right thing to do.”

El-Sayed cast his ballot in early voting. Michigan is one of the few Senate races this cycle that Republicans believe they can flip from blue to red, making the contest one of the most watched in the nation.

The race has been marred by explosive character attacks, identity politics, and an unprecedented level of negative advertising.

As Rogers cast his ballot, across the street was a giant balloon figure of Jeffrey Epstein, standing over 10 feet tall, holding a sign reading “Mike Rogers bankrolled Epstein class.”

Mailers in the state have contained personal attacks and stoked racial politics. A group supporting El-Sayed aired a controversial TV ad claiming the high cost of groceries was the result of Israel.

Rogers on Tuesday reminded voters of El-Sayed’s stance.

“They understand the risk of having the Democrat Socialists of America have their first statewide candidate going into the United States Senate,” he said.

El Sayed said he’s not a DSA member, but his policies very much align, including Medicare for all, abolishing ICE, ending military aid to Israel and dramatically taxing the rich.

President Trump has weighed in, calling El-Sayed a “jihadist” and a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, while Vice President JD Vance called him a “psychopath.”

After Stevens endorsed Rogers, many Democrats came out slamming her and her fiancé. Turkish, a 39-year-old disability lawyer and political fundraiser, is Jewish and disavowed El-Sayed’s rhetoric on Israel that he says makes Jews unsafe. He endorsed Rogers a few days before Stevens did.

Stevens said such talk was sexist.

“Some critics have also dragged my fiancé into this, suggesting he or others must have made my decision for me,” she wrote in a lengthy post on X. “Think about what that says. A woman can serve in Congress, run statewide, and fight for her convictions, and still be told that when she makes a choice people dislike, someone else must be pulling the strings.

“That is sexism dressed up as political analysis.”

And her mother, Maria Marcotte, defended her, telling The Post: “We’re not the kind of women to be brainwashed.”

The RealClearPolitics voting average has El-Sayed ahead but the polls were conducted before Stevens publicly endorsed Rogers.

Many voters in the state have already cast their ballot: more than 2.4 million out of nearly 8 million registered voters.

news.originalContent:
Shrimpers worry about fuel costs, tariffs and Trump’s proposed cuts to the agency that provides vital weather data.

Mount Pleasant, South Carolina – For Mark Marhefka, the weather can be the difference between a profitable fishing trip and a dangerous one.

As a shrimper and fisherman for 49 years, Marhefka relies on forecasts, weather buoys and data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to decide when it is safe to take his boats offshore. With storms and warm water temperatures disrupting this year’s fishing season, he worries that President Donald Trump’s proposed funding cuts could further reduce the services fishermen depend on.

“They’ve already started cutting back on NOAA, and they’re looking to do more in this next fiscal year,” Marhefka, who owns Abundant Seafood, told Al Jazeera. “It’s definitely something that we need to fight against.”

Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, NOAA has lost roughly 20 percent of its workforce, according to an analysis of federal employment data. The administration’s proposed 2027 budget would cut funding for ocean monitoring and terminate a programme supporting regional ocean observations.

But the weather is only one of the pressures facing South Carolina shrimpers as they head to the polls on Tuesday for the US midterm elections.

Rising fuel prices, equipment costs and competition from imported shrimp are weighing on people who make their living from the water.

Marhefka believes Democrats could address these pressures better than Republicans.

“Fuel costs have doubled since Trump has been back in office,” said Marhefka. “I voted Democrat because I really think Annie Andrews is going to help South Carolina.”

At an election-eve rally in Charleston on Monday, the state’s Democratic Senate candidate, Annie Andrews, sought to appeal to voters like Marhefka, arguing that her campaign would address the financial pressures facing coastal communities.

“I’m fighting for a South Carolina that we can afford,” Andrews said to the crowd. “I’m fighting to lower the damn diesel for our farmers and our fishermen and our shrimpers.”

Although shrimpers make up a small share of South Carolina’s electorate, their concerns raise bigger questions about the cost of doing business and retirement planning.

John Henry Middleton, an 81-year-old fisherman who has been shrimping for about 50 years, is an undecided voter. He says he is frustrated with both parties, arguing that politicians make promises but fail to work together on issues affecting common people.

“I want to see them get together and work for the good of the people,” he told Al Jazeera.

His concerns as he heads to the ballot box on Tuesday include the cost of living and whether he will have enough money to support himself in retirement. He said he has paid taxes and worked for decades, but still has to work at 81.

Kevin S, who declined to give his last name, works at Geechee Seafood on Shem Creek and said he plans to vote Republican on Tuesday. He said many people in the fishing industry lean Republican because they see government regulation as an obstacle to making a living.

“It’s a pretty regulated industry. A lot of red tape, a lot of extreme permits,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that some fishing permits can cost thousands of dollars.

Kevin added that rising fuel prices have increased the cost of running his business, but he doesn’t closely follow the factors driving those increases.

When asked whether the war in Iran was contributing to higher prices, he said he didn’t know enough about the issue to say. Instead, he pointed to Trump’s efforts to increase domestic energy production as a reason he thinks Republicans are better placed to address fuel costs.

He also believes many blue-collar workers share this view, but emphasised that industry support for Republicans does not necessarily mean enthusiasm for the party.

“I just don’t really trust Democrats as much to make the best financial decisions,” he said. “It’s not that a lot of people love the Republican Party. It’s more of a lesser of two evils.”

The pressures facing shrimpers are also evident in the dwindling number of businesses around Shem Creek, a historic fishing area near Charleston. Cindy and Taylor Tarvin, co-owners of Tarvin Seafood, estimate that only about eight shrimpers remain in the area. They say the decline reflects how difficult it has become to make a living in the industry.

“Younger captains can make a living, but not a lavish one,” Cindy Tarvin told Al Jazeera.

The Tarvins said their diesel costs rose sharply this year. They started the year paying $2.71 per gallon (3.78 litres), but by late September they were paying $5.99 per gallon. The American Automobile Association (AAA) reported that South Carolina’s average retail diesel price reached a record $6.17 that month.

Maintenance and equipment costs have also risen, adding to the financial strain on boat owners.

“There will always be a demand for watermen and what they produce. What scale they’re able to do it at is the big question,” Taylor Tarvin told Al Jazeera.

The Tarvins agree that one of the biggest challenges is the volume of imported shrimp entering the US market. Shrimp from abroad is often sold at lower prices, making it difficult for domestic fishermen to compete.

They said the influx of imports has contributed to falling prices and razor-thin profit margins, forcing some local boats out of business.

The competition extends well beyond South Carolina. According to the Southern Shrimp Alliance, the United States imported 1.59 billion pounds, or about 721,000 tonnes, of frozen warmwater shrimp in 2025, a 2 percent increase from the previous year.

In July 2026, the Trump administration imposed additional tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on imported shrimp from major suppliers including India, Ecuador, Indonesia, Vietnam and Thailand.

Trump’s tariffs on imported shrimp initially raised hopes among domestic shrimpers that foreign products would become more expensive and local catch more competitive. But the Tarvins said they have yet to see a meaningful benefit in the prices they receive, and are unsure whether they ever will.

There is another complication. Tariffs on imported steel, aluminium and products made from those materials have increased the cost of maintaining boats.

“So all of the pieces and parts that go into keeping a fishing boat running and keeping the equipment replaceable are affected by tariffs,” Cindy said.

For Marhefka, rising costs are part of a broader frustration with the country’s direction. He says he tries not to discuss politics often, but has heard growing frustration from those who voted for Trump and feel their circumstances have worsened.

“I just don’t think that we can go and handle another two more years of this,” he said. “We’re just getting squeezed too hard.”

news.originalContent:
Survivors of attacks on displacement camps in Darfur recall the lives they built, and the violence that forced them to flee.

In a small house in Omdurman, Hassan Saber Jumaa, a senior administrator at the Zamzam displacement camp in Sudan, sat on a simple wooden chair. He scrolled through his phone, looking for any photograph he might have of Zamzam, which is near el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, and once sheltered hundreds of thousands.

He found nothing. Jumaa explained that his old phone was looted during last year’s attack by Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces on the camp. Pointing to the bare walls around him, Jumaa said that all he has left are his memories of the camp, and the people who once called it home.

Zamzam, established in 2004, was home to generations of people displaced by western Sudan’s Darfur war, which began in 2003 and continued for nearly two decades. Alongside Abu Shouk camp and al-Salam camp, Zamzam formed part of one of Darfur’s largest concentrations of displaced people.

Jumaa recalled a bustling community, with its market open every day, and children walking to school.

Zamzam continued as a refuge for civilians until Sudan’s current war, which began in 2023. The RSF, fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces and its allies, captured the camp in April 2025, after months of attacks. Famine had been confirmed in the camp in August 2024.

Mukhtar Musa, a survivor of the assault, watched the community he knew descend into starvation and violence. He said restrictions on the movement of goods had exhausted food supplies, leaving some residents with little choice but to eat animal feed and peanut shells.

Umm Kulthum Ali Saleh described the months before the final attack as the hardest of her life. The RSF siege on Zamzam stopped goods from entering. She searched for food every morning, and recalled seeing women cooking grass and mixing mud with flour to bake bread.

Saleh believes the blockade was not merely a military measure, but a deliberate way to weaken the camp’s residents in advance of the final offensive, and Zamzam’s fall.

On April 11, the RSF launched a three-day assault using cars, camels, and horses, burning straw homes and health facilities.

A United Nations Human Rights Office report documented at least 1,013 civilians killed, including 319 who were summarily executed in homes, markets, schools, clinics, and mosques. The report documented other abuses, including rape, gang rape, sexual slavery, and other forms of sexual violence, particularly targeting the Zaghawa community.

Musa was a witness to some of those mass killings, and said he saw RSF fighters kill civilians while chanting religious slogans. He described seeing bodies scattered around the main market and near schools, and said fighters continued pursuing civilians along roads leading out of the camp.

Saleh also recalled seeing bodies littering the roads, with only chickens, donkeys, and sheep wandering among the abandoned buildings.

The attack forced tens of thousands to flee Zamzam, with many remaining in the el-Fasher area, and others fleeing south to Tawila and Dar al-Salam.

The violence continued to engulf el-Fasher and its surrounding displacement camps over the following months.

With Zamzam under its control, the RSF launched an attack on el-Fasher in August 2025, and soon captured the Abu Shouk camp.

The UN Human Rights Office said at least 40 displaced people were killed inside Abu Shouk, while 19 others were injured. The International Organization for Migration reported that at least 500 residents fled the camp that day.

The RSF captured el-Fasher itself on October 26, 2025. More than 6,000 people are believed to have been killed in the attack, in el-Fasher as well as on escape routes out of the city. Survivors of attacks on displacement camps in Darfur recall the lives they built, and the violence that forced them to flee.

In a small house in Omdurman, Hassan Saber Jumaa, a senior administrator at the Zamzam displacement camp in Sudan, sat on a simple wooden chair. He scrolled through his phone, looking for any photograph he might have of Zamzam, which is near el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, and once sheltered hundreds of thousands.

He found nothing. Jumaa explained that his old phone was looted during last year’s attack by Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces on the camp. Pointing to the bare walls around him, Jumaa said that all he has left are his memories of the camp, and the people who once called it home.

Zamzam, established in 2004, was home to generations of people displaced by western Sudan’s Darfur war, which began in 2003 and continued for nearly two decades. Alongside Abu Shouk camp and al-Salam camp, Zamzam formed part of one of Darfur’s largest concentrations of displaced people.

Jumaa recalled a bustling community, with its market open every day, and children walking to school.

Zamzam continued as a refuge for civilians until Sudan’s current war, which began in 2023. The RSF, fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces and its allies, captured the camp in April 2025, after months of attacks. Famine had been confirmed in the camp in August 2024.

Mukhtar Musa, a survivor of the assault, watched the community he knew descend into starvation and violence. He said restrictions on the movement of goods had exhausted food supplies, leaving some residents with little choice but to eat animal feed and peanut shells.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by Loren Orr/Getty Images for MoveOn)

Idaho Freedom Foundation (IFF) made national news in October when The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) highlighted our work. While their report revealed the importance of IFF’s Freedom and Spending indexes, it also exposed key obstacles to advancing conservative policy in the Gem State.

The report, titled “I Went Back to Idaho to See How the Hard-Right Transformed This Deep Red State,” seemed to be angled around the “far-right” taking over Idaho. But instead, the outlet illuminated the powerful special interests — and the legislators beholden to them — fighting Idaho’s conservative values.

On a more positive note, the WSJ also reported on IFF’s conservative priorities and highlighted our Freedom and Spending Indexes.

The WSJ turned to Republican state Rep. Jack Nelsen, who “proudly” received F ratings from IFF on both indexes, for his take on Idaho’s political landscape.

“Organizations like the [Idaho] Freedom Foundation have had a huge impact on how legislators vote, and how some of my constituents think,” Nelsen admitted to the WSJ.

He also told the outlet he has “not signed the Republican platform … as an elected Republican” (Nelsen announced earlier in 2026 he would not seek reelection). He was censured by the Blaine and Lincoln County Republican Central Committees in 2025.

He voted against a myriad of conservative bills, such as House Bill 239, which in part mandated that school districts alert parents before any educational instruction concerning human sexuality. IFF gave the bill a positive (+2) rating.

Nelsen also opposed House Bill 352, which aimed to amend the Parental Rights in Education statute by banning classroom instruction on gender identity or sexual orientation in K-12 education. IFF gave the bill a positive (+1) rating.

The WSJ also spoke with Republican state Rep. Clint Hostetler and pointed to his IFF Freedom Index score. He has an A rating on the Freedom Index and an A+ rating on the Spending Index.

“One of the issues the Idaho Freedom Foundation has supported is a hard stance on immigration,” the WSJ noted.

Indeed, IFF’s 2027 Freedom and Family Agenda specifically highlights illegal immigration and the costs it imposes on taxpayers, as well as the need to ensure only citizens in Idaho vote in our elections. IFF has also supported good immigration legislation, such as House Bill 660 to mandate local and state law enforcement agencies record and verify the nationality and immigration status of arrested individuals. IFF gave it a positive (+1 rating); IFF has also made our stance on illegal immigration clear in numerous articles.

The WSJ’s report highlighted pushback from some dairy industry operators over conservative immigration policies. The dairy industry, with groups like Idaho Dairy Men, has a powerful lobbying arm. Idaho special interest groups are alive and well in the Gem State — but IFF serves as a crucial voice for all Idahoans.

Even a New York City-based outlet recognizes IFF’s influence in advancing pro-freedom policies. Though the report at times seemed to suggest Idahoans could be gravitating toward more moderate politics, the outlet still framed the story as though the “hard right” has an iron grip on Idaho.

Neither angle appears to accurately reflect the Gem State. In reality, it would seem Idaho’s government is not as conservative as most Idahoans, which many legislators — and executive officials — have demonstrated by supporting wasteful spending and killing effective, conservative bills.

The WSJ played a video showing IFF President Ron Nate cautioning, “Idaho is under threat always from becoming the next blue state.” Not because Idaho residents support the policies of their blue-state neighbors, but because legislators routinely vote against Idahoans’ interests (just take a look at IFF’s 2026 Pork Report).

The danger facing Idaho isn’t a hard-right transformation, but a milquetoast brand of establishment politics paving the way for a socialist takeover of our institutions — precisely what happened in Colorado, and what IFF is fighting here in the Gem State.

The national media took notice, underscoring the importance of IFF’s mission to defeat socialism and hold government accountable. We will oblige.

Eireann is a local government policy analyst at Idaho Freedom Foundation. She was previously a reporter and editor at Daily Caller. She majored in journalism at Liberty University.

The views and opinions expressed in this commentary are those of the author and do not reflect the official position of the Daily Caller.

news.originalContent:
With neither bloc near a majority, Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties hold the key to Israel’s next government.

Israel’s election results are due to be certified on Wednesday, but with both leading blocs falling short of a parliamentary majority, negotiations remain deadlocked.

As things stand, the right-wing coalition of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured 53 seats in the October 27 vote, while the self-styled Zionist opposition alliance led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot had 48. A majority requires 61 seats in the 120-strong Knesset. The 19 remaining seats went to the two Arab-led lists – the Joint List and Ra’am, or the United Arab List.

Netanyahu’s camp has been accused of seeking to delegitimise the results after launching a series of largely discounted claims that the vote for the Arab parties, which scored their best-ever electoral performance, had been manipulated by foreign interference.

Despite their historic showing that was boosted by an unprecedented surge in voter turnout, the two Arab-led lists remain politically isolated. And while there have been indications that they would be prepared to support, or at least not oppose, an Eisenkot-led government, their backing remains contentious within the opposition – a broad and increasingly fractious alliance that also includes parties led by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, left-winger Yair Golan and right-winger Avigdor Lieberman.

After a meeting on Tuesday, the main opposition leaders issued a statement announcing that they were preparing to “act immediately” to replace Netanyahu’s governing coalition “with a national emergency government and translate the clear parliamentary majority in the Knesset into action”. Yet, the statement did not specify how they would reach the majority that would ultimately depend on them allying with either the Arab-led lists or two ultra-Orthodox parties, which have historically supported Netanyahu in return for shielding some of their members from military service.

“Essentially, we’re both on track to a government, and nowhere near being able to form one,” Israeli pollster Mitchell Barak told Al Jazeera.

Though informal negotiations are widely reported to have begun, official talks on establishing a governing coalition will start only after the results are certified on Wednesday. Netanyahu’s Likud party has already mooted refusing to recognise the results, citing its continuing claims of irregularities in the Arab vote. Those allegations have been investigated and discounted by police, while a separate probe by the internal security service, the Shin Bet, remains ongoing.

Once the results are certified, President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with all the parties to determine which member of the Knesset, not necessarily a party leader, is best placed to form a government.

Herzog, who lost to Netanyahu after an especially bitter contest in 2015, has found himself in the unusual position of having to decide who should be given the first opportunity to form a government, while simultaneously considering the prime minister’s longstanding request for a pardon in his ongoing corruption trial.

One of Herzog’s options is to ask the Arab parties to recommend Eisenkot. If selected, the leader of the centrist Yashar party will initially have 28 days to assemble a coalition, a period that can be extended by 14 days. Should he fail, Herzog can then invite another candidate to try.

For his part, Netanyahu on Monday argued that Likud’s first-place finish, with 27 seats, gave him a mandate to lead the next government. “We aim to form a broad government with our partners and with any other party that wishes to join, provided they do not support terrorism,” he said.

Still, it is unlikely he will be able to command a majority without entering an alliance with the Arab parties that he has consistently vilified, or a large-scale wave of defections from the opposition.

Whatever the state of the negotiations, the new Knesset is due to be sworn in on November 10.

Barak said coordination within the opposition appeared minimal, while personal animosities between Netanyahu and Herzog further complicated already fraught negotiations.

“It’s really not clear who’s talking to who,” he added.

“Earlier this week, they named [Bennett’s running mate] Lapid as their choice of speaker, which was apparently news to both Eisenkot and Bennett. Equally, Netanyahu now has to appeal to his political rival, Herzog, both to be given the responsibility of forming a government and to be pardoned before any conviction,” Barak continued.

“All the while, he’s claiming that the Arab parties cannot be considered legitimate partners in government, which makes it almost impossible for anyone to form a coalition with them.”

However, the extent to which the efforts to delegitimise the Arab parties may succeed remains uncertain. Ra’am served as a central plank of the Bennett-Lapid coalition in 2021–22, the first time an independent Arab party had formally joined an Israeli government, with public pressure to do so again growing.

Over the weekend, thousands rallied in Tel Aviv calling upon Eisenkot to make a deal with the Arab parties that reflected the overwhelming number of votes cast against Netanyahu’s governing coalition. However, following the meeting between the opposition leaders on Tuesday, sources within the Joint List told Al Jazeera they were not expecting to be invited to support the bloc anytime soon.

Instead, speculation has turned to the possibility of one of the two ultra-Orthodox parties – Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), and particularly the latter – defecting to the opposition and backing Eisenkot.

Neither Shas nor UTJ have had straightforward relationships with Netanyahu’s governing coalition. In fact, it was the withdrawal of their parliamentary support in May, following what they saw as the coalition’s failure to pass a draft law exempting some of their ultra-Orthodox members from military service, that fundamentally weakened its majority in parliament.

“There are rumours that the Ashkenazi [Jews, who make up the bulk of the UTJ membership] are ready to break with Netanyahu and go to Eisenkot,” political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg told Al Jazeera.

“I am sceptical, but even that would still leave them short of an overall majority, so they would still need support from one of the Arab parties, even if that is Ra’am supporting them from outside a formal coalition,” he said of the parliamentary arithmetic.

Hanging over all, however, are developments tied to Israel’s deep and longstanding alliance with the United States.

Barak said the entire government-formation process risked being disrupted by the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, which could weaken Israel’s foremost ally, President Donald Trump, or be overtaken entirely by renewed war with Iran.

Netanyahu, particularly, went to pains during the election campaign to stress his relationship with Trump, whose Republican Party faces a tough race to keep hold of Congress.

Equally, both Trump’s rhetoric as well as the renewed build-up of US forces in the region may all signal the beginning of renewed conflict with Israel’s regional nemesis, Iran.

“Netanyahu cannot form a coalition,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera. “It’s a numbers game, and he just doesn’t have the numbers – no amount of talking and planning can change that, but an emergency could, and in Israel, there’s no more popular an emergency than one involving Iran.”

In such an instance, he speculated that the incumbent could ask the opposition to fall in behind him, but that would raise the possibility of a former captain dictating war policy to former generals.

“There’s also the possibility that, however you want to define it, Israel has a successful war against Iran. That leads to a surge in popularity for Netanyahu when negotiations on a coalition resume, or [him] calling unnecessary, fresh elections,” said Mekelberg.

news.originalContent:
Police are investigating the motive in murder of MKP coordinator as political killings rise during municipal elections.

An organiser from an opposition party has been killed in South Africa’s KwaZulu-Natal province, raising concerns about political violence before Wednesday’s local government elections.

⁠Senior police spokesman Robert Netshiunda said on Tuesday that a murder investigation had been opened after Lastborn Shazi – identified by the uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) – was shot dead late on Monday at his home while on a Zoom call coordinating the party’s election campaign.

Police are investigating the motive, Netshiunda said.

South African police said last weekend that 20 murders involving political representatives, party members and supporters had been recorded during the municipal election period.
